identity.title: When Selection Meets Intervention: Additional Complexities in Causal Discovery

problem.claim: Interventional causal discovery must account for selective enrollment of subjects into experiments.

gap.claim: Existing interventional causal-discovery approaches do not address selection bias because intervention timing and location can produce different statistical patterns.

contributions.claim: Introduces a graphical model representing both the observed intervention world and the counterfactual selection world.

Characterizes the model’s Markov property and proposes a provably sound algorithm for identifying causal relations and selection mechanisms up to an equivalence class from soft-intervention data with unknown targets.

stated_novelty.claim: The stated new distinction is explicitly modeling where interventions occur in the observed world versus where selection occurs before intervention in the counterfactual world.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report synthetic and real-world experiments in which their algorithm effectively identifies true causal relations despite selection bias.

narrative_sequence.summary: Selective enrollment is common in drug trials, app A/B tests, and gene perturbation studies.
Ignoring selection bias can produce incorrect causal-discovery results, while existing paradigms still fail to address it.
The abstract attributes the difficulty to differences in when and where interventions occur, which alter statistical patterns.
The paper introduces a two-world graphical model, derives its Markov property, proposes an algorithm, and reports synthetic and real-world demonstrations.

source_observation.claim: The paper links its model design directly to a specific distinction between intervention and selection contexts, then aligns the algorithm’s stated scope with soft interventions and unknown targets.

lessons.interpretation: A concrete causal or statistical distinction can motivate both the representation and the precise problem boundary.
lessons.application: When proposing a model, explicitly map each added variable or world to the mechanism it represents and state the data regime the resulting method targets.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the application has no defensible separation between the modeled contexts or lacks data supporting the proposed regime.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the assumptions, exact Markov property, equivalence class, algorithm details, or what “effectively” means quantitatively.
The real-world datasets, baselines, metrics, and experimental conditions are not reported.
